directed acyclic graphs (dags) directed-acyclic-graphs-dags  represent bounded agent work as explicit dependencies, enabling reproducible scheduling, parallel branches, and precise restart boundaries. a directed acyclic graph models tasks as nodes and dependencies as edges without allowing a path back to an earlier node. it fits workflows whose overall structure is known before execution, even when individual nodes use probabilistic models. the graph exposes the critical path and makes prerequisites visible to schedulers and reviewers. a dag is not a complete model for open-ended agent behavior. replanning and repeated critique require a bounded subworkflow or an external state machine. separate the graph definition from each execution instance so retries, artifact versions, and task status do not mutate the intended dependency structure. a prototype may implement dependencies as ordinary function calls. draw the actual graph to expose accidental serialization and missing validation steps. production persists node outcomes and schedules only ready nodes. make artifact identity include relevant input versions so cached output cannot survive a material source change. at scale, agentic state machines agentic-state-machines  make agent progress an explicit set of states, guarded transitions, and durable events so every action has a permitted execution context. an agentic state machine defines named states and the events that can move a run between them. states represent operational facts such as awaiting evidence, ready for review, or committed; they should not claim to expose the model's private reasoning. transition guards enforce business invariants outside the model. the model can propose an event or classify an observation, but deterministic transition code decides whether it is legal. persist the state version alongside the transition event to prevent concurrent workers from both advancing the same run. state design is therefore a concurrency and authorization decision as much as an orchestration technique. a proof of concept often uses booleans such as approved and finished. replace ambiguous combinations with a small explicit state model before adding external writes. production adds transition guards, optimistic concurrency, expiration events, and an operator view. terminal states must explain whether work succeeded, failed, or was cancelled. enterprise deployments require machine-version migration and compatibility for old runs. a new release cannot assume that every persisted execution starts at the first state. state hierarchical orchestration hierarchical-orchestration  delegate through supervisory layers that preserve domain ownership, limit context, and return evidence-rich results to a single accountable decision maker. hierarchical orchestration organizes agents into supervisors and subordinate workers. a top-level supervisor chooses domains and integrates their results; each domain supervisor decomposes work within a narrower capability boundary. the hierarchy is useful when different teams own different tools, policies, and evaluation criteria. every delegation adds latency and a chance to lose constraints. supervisors should pass explicit contracts rather than conversational instructions, and workers should return findings with provenance rather than polished summaries alone. hierarchy should follow real decision ownership. replicating an organization chart without independent responsibilities produces unnecessary layers. a prototype can use one supervisor and two workers to test whether bounded delegation improves quality or tool isolation. production needs delegation identifiers, depth limits, budget inheritance, and cancellation propagation. a child cannot expand dynamic routing dynamic-routing  select the appropriate agent or workflow from request intent, capability, authorization, and uncertainty while keeping routing decisions observable and reversible. asynchronous agent execution asynchronous-agent-execution  move long-running agent work into durable jobs with explicit acceptance, progress, cancellation, and completion semantics. asynchronous execution separates accepting a request from completing its work. the service returns an operation identifier after durable acceptance, while workers process the operation independently of the user's connection. this is an api contract, not merely a background thread: clients need a reliable way to observe status and retrieve the final result. the central difficulty is ownership across failures. a queue may deliver a job more than once, a worker can lose its lease, and a client can retry submission after an uncertain response. use durable operation records, deduplication identities, and idempotent side effects to make these ordinary events safe. a prototype can use an in-process task for disposable work. confirm that losing the process and its work is acceptable before choosing that shortcut. production persists acceptance before acknowledgement, separates job state from queue state, and gives clients documented polling or notification behavior. cancellation is cooperative unless the underlying operation supports stronger guarantees. at enterprise scale, fair queues, tenant quotas, backpressure, and bounded worker concurrency protect interactive systems. measure queue age agent inter-communication (a2a) agent-inter-communication-a2a  interoperate across independently operated agents through explicit capability discovery, task lifecycle contracts, authenticated deadlines, accepted modalities, artifact schemas, and cancellation semantics. it does not require agents to expose their prompts, private reasoning, or internal orchestration implementation. the agent2agent protocol provides a concrete interoperability model including agent cards, messages, tasks, and artifacts. protocol versions evolve, so deployments should pin and negotiate supported plan-and-execute pattern plan-and-execute-pattern  separate deliberate task planning from controlled execution, validating dependencies and revising only the parts invalidated by new evidence. the plan-and-execute pattern creates an explicit task plan before carrying out its steps. the planner proposes objectives, dependencies, tool requirements, and acceptance criteria; the executor performs approved steps and records observations. a plan is a hypothesis about how to finish the task, not permission to perform every conceivable action. separating these roles makes long tasks inspectable and allows deterministic validation before expensive or consequential work begins. plans should contain bounded operational steps rather than hidden reasoning transcripts. replanning is triggered by react framework (reasoning + acting) react-framework-reasoning-acting  alternate bounded action proposals with tool observations, allowing an agent to adapt its next step while application code controls authority and termination. react combines reasoning about a task with actions that obtain observations from external tools. architecturally, the useful property is feedback: the next action can respond to actual evidence instead of assuming every required fact in advance. the runtime should expose structured action proposals and observations, not depend on storing or revealing private
